findings: genericSearch.ts's excludeDeleted() hardcodes the column name 'deleted_at', but the users table has no deleted_at column at all (only is_deleted BOOLEAN) — the exclusion filter can never match anything on 'users'.

Because the ORM is configured with unknownColumnMode: 'silent-skip', the where('deleted_at', 'IS', null) clause against the users table is silently dropped instead of erroring, so search('users', …) runs with no soft-delete filter whatsoever — this is the direct cause of deleted accounts appearing in search results.

The orders and users tables use two incompatible soft-delete conventions (deleted_at TIMESTAMP vs is_deleted BOOLEAN) with no shared column name or adapter layer, yet genericSearch.ts's excludeDeleted() is applied uniformly to both tables as if they were schema-compatible.

The silent-skip unknown-column mode is a global configuration for 'all search endpoints', not scoped to the optional-filter use case it was introduced for — it also masks structural/required filters like the soft-delete predicate, converting what should be a loud failure (missing/wrong column) into a silent correctness bug.

There is no per-table mapping or abstraction for soft-delete semantics (e.g. a table-to-soft-delete-strategy registry); excludeDeleted() assumes a single global convention, so adding any future table with a different deletion scheme will reproduce the same bug.

The users table's is_deleted design loses information relative to orders' deleted_at (no timestamp of when a user was deleted), so even after fixing the filter, users soft-deletes carry less audit/recovery capability than orders soft-deletes — a further inconsistency beyond just the query bug.

Nothing in the described system (types, tests, schema validation, or the query builder) enforces that excludeDeleted() references a column that actually exists on the target table, so the same class of bug (filter silently no-ops due to column mismatch) can recur for any other filter, not just deleted_at.
